prompt.context: Home Improvement Co. is a major home improvement retailer in the U.S. that sells tools, construction products, appliances, and services. Since 2020, the company has struggled to hit their profitability targets and are looking for possible solutions. Our client, the CFO of the company, has hired us to come up with a plan to reverse this trajectory and return the company to its profitability level from 3 years ago. The company had $50B in revenue in 2021 and operates through 3 distribution channels: in-store, buy online pick-up in-store, and deliver to home. The home improvement retail industry has been experiencing growth the last few years as consumers are spending more time at home during the pandemic and focusing a bigger share of their budget on home projects. Home Improvement Co. has dozens of suppliers for each category they sell. Due to world supply chain constraints and increased demand, lead times for lower-turnover products have increased dramatically.
prompt.question: What is driving the decline in profitability, and what plan would you recommend to return the company to its 2019 profitability level?

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue of Home Improvement Co.?
What is the target profitability level?
clarifying_info.a: The same level of profitability as 3 years ago, in 2019.

clarifying_info.q: What markets does the company operate in?
How many distribution channels does the company have?
clarifying_info.a: Three: in-store, buy online pick-up in-store, and deliver to home.

clarifying_info.q: How does the competitive landscape look?
clarifying_info.a: The home improvement retail industry has been growing as consumers spend more time at home; no specific competitor data is provided upfront.

exhibits.title: Revenue and Costs (2019-21)
exhibits.shows: A grouped bar chart showing Revenue and Costs side by side for 2019, 2020, and 2021 in billions of US dollars.

exhibits.title: Cost Breakdown (2019-21)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart breaking total costs into four components — COGS, Rent, Marketing, and Salaries — for 2019, 2020, and 2021 in billions of US dollars.

exhibits.title: 2022 Projections
exhibits.shows: A table showing historical Revenue and cost line items (COGS, Rent, Marketing, Salaries) for 2019-2021 plus 2022 forecasts, with Revenue projected to grow 20% vs. 2021 and Rent, Marketing, Salaries each growing 25% vs. 2021; 2022 COGS is left blank as a question mark.

framework: Financial Considerations: Revenue (change in units sold, change in average price) vs. Costs (fixed costs such as Rent, Overhead, Insurance, SG&A; variable costs such as Materials, Labor, other COGS)
Market and Global Trends: Number of major competitors and recent performance; new technology and market trends; global supply chain considerations; impact of general inflation
Customer Needs: Changes in customer preferences during the pandemic; changes in overall number of customers; customer share-of-wallet over the last 3 years

questions.prompt: What conclusions can you draw from Exhibit 1?
questions.guidance: Basic: Both revenue and costs rose from 2019 to 2021, but costs grew faster than revenue, causing profit to fall from $7B in 2019 to $5B in 2021. Second-order: Profit margins shrank aggressively — candidates should calculate profit margin for 2019 and 2021 and note the trend.

math.setup: Profit = Revenue - Costs; Profit Margin = (Revenue - Costs) / Revenue
math.answer: Profit dropped from $7B (20% margin) in 2019 to $5B (10% margin) in 2021 — a $2B decline and a halving of the profit margin.

questions.prompt: Given that costs are the main driver, can you analyze the cost breakdown in Exhibit 2?
questions.guidance: Basic: All cost lines increased, but COGS is the dominant driver. Second-order: Candidates should compute absolute and percentage change per line. COGS grew $9B (+75%) and accounts for 53% of the total $17B cost increase (9/17). Strong candidates will identify COGS as the primary lever to address.

math.setup: Absolute change = 2021 value - 2019 value; Percentage change = absolute change / 2019 value
steps: COGS share of total cost increase: 9/17 = 53%
math.answer: COGS is the biggest absolute driver (+$9B, +75%) and accounts for 53% of the total cost increase.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3: Revenue will grow 20% in 2022 vs. 2021, and Rent, Marketing, and Salaries will each grow 25% vs. 2021. What is the maximum COGS Home Improvement Co. can incur in 2022 to achieve a 20% profit margin?
questions.guidance: Candidates must back-solve for COGS using the profit margin formula. Revenue for 2022 = 50 * 1.20 = $60B. Target profit = 20% * 60 = $12B. Fixed costs in 2022 = (8+8+8)*1.25 = $30B. Maximum COGS = 60 - 12 - 30 = $18B. Note: current 2021 COGS is $21B, so the company must reduce COGS by $3B — a dramatic renegotiation with suppliers is required.

math.setup: Profit Margin = (Revenue - Total Costs) / Revenue = 20%; solve for COGS
math.answer: Maximum COGS in 2022 is $18B (down from $21B in 2021, a required reduction of $3B or ~14%).

brainstorming.prompt: Before deep-diving into analysis, what could be drivers of decreasing profitability?

categories.name: Decreasing Revenue
ideas: Decreasing quantity of units sold — due to declining customer purchasing power or customers becoming more cautious about expenditures
Decreasing average price of units sold — price war with competitors forcing Home Improvement Co. to lower prices
Decreasing number of customers — due to sell-outs, long wait times for orders, or poor customer experience

categories.name: Increasing Costs
ideas: Variable costs: increase in materials/supply costs due to worldwide supply shortage
Variable costs: increase in wages due to worker shortage and decreased worker safety during the pandemic
Fixed costs: increase in overhead costs to stay competitive against competitors

brainstorming.prompt: What are the reasons for increased COGS in the last few years, and how can Home Improvement Co. work to decrease them?

categories.name: Reasons — External Factors
ideas: Global supply chain shortage driving up raw material costs
Loss of bargaining power relative to suppliers as demand exceeds supply across the industry
Competitors outpacing growth, causing suppliers to raise prices for Home Improvement Co.

categories.name: Reasons — Internal Factors
ideas: Rapid growth creating difficulty finding qualified labor
Investment in more expensive production methods to compensate for labor shortages

categories.name: How to Decrease — External
ideas: Renegotiate supplier agreements with minimum SLAs and long-term fixed-price adjustments
Invest in verticalization — produce own raw materials to reduce dependency on external suppliers

categories.name: How to Decrease — Internal
ideas: Launch a training and talent-retention program to build qualified labor pipeline
Negotiate adoption of new technologies to reduce production costs

recommendation: To return profit margin to 20% by 2022, Home Improvement Co. must reduce COGS from $21B to $18B — a $3B reduction.
We recommend renegotiating supplier agreements with defined SLAs and long-term fixed-price adjustments, and investing in new technology to reduce production costs.
risks: Suppliers may be unable or unwilling to change SLAs due to an aggravation of the global supply chain crisis.
Fixed-cost investment in new technology may prove ineffective or take longer than expected to yield savings.
next_steps: Map potential alternative suppliers to ensure supply continuity and strengthen negotiating leverage.
Develop a verticalization plan to integrate part of the production process into the company's own supply chain as a contingency.
